subject: Regarding the difference between model$summary.fitted.values and model$summary.random

messages.author: b431df4437cb4a5f
messages.subject: Regarding the difference between model$summary.fitted.values and model$summary.random
parts:
Hello- I have been working through several books on disease mapping and have run into something I am not at all clear on. I am hoping the group can help clear this up for me.
In Blangiardo and Cameletti, Spatial and Spatiotemporal  Bayesian Models in R-INLA, they utilize the familiar London suicide dataset to calculate "borough-specific" relative risks by exponentiating the area specific residuals from the first n rows (S+U) from the $summary.random$id returns. In Morgana, Geospatial Health Data, Modelling and Visualization with R-INLA and Shiny, relative risk is calculated by $summary.fitted.values.  Now clearly these values do not match in my models and I don't think I would expect them to. So I am a little unclear on what the difference between these two relative risks are and what that specifically means. Is one just for the random effects and the other for random and fixed effects? I have looked through the discussion board for the answer and it is likely the answer is right in front of me and I am not seeing it.

Many thanks,

Dan J.

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Regarding the difference between model$summary.fitted.values and model$summary.random
parts:
I think this is what you ask for.

if you have a random variable x, and y=exp(x),

then

E(y) != exp(E(x))

but the quantiles of 'y' will be exp of the quantiles of 'x'.

so the quantiles will be correct but the mean will be a little off.

this is the B&C approach.

for Moraga, then the density for the fitted values are computed as
y=exp(x), from the density of 'x', using a change of variable formula,
hence for the fitted values then E() and Var() will also be correct.

Best
H
